hook: Before you even reach the description, SCP-106's file shows its containment procedures being rewritten, and failing. Treat the revision notes as part of the story; they tell you more about the threat than any adjective could. Be aware that the later sections describe deliberate injury to young people in clinical detail.
whyItMatters:
106 is one of the classic Keter-class pursuers, and the image at its center, a rotting figure that sinks into walls and floors and drags people into a space only it can reach, is the kind of idea that sticks with readers long after the details fade.

It is also an early showcase for a structural trick: keeping superseded containment procedures on the page. Instead of one authoritative set of rules, you get a record of attempts, which turns a plain report into a short history of losing.
thingsToNotice:
The stacked revisions are a clever device: each old version is stamped discontinued with a reason, and in the second case the fluid agitation system actually spread the corrosion and caused several breaches at once. The final version's odd specifics (forty layers of lead-lined steel, randomly spaced struts, sixteen fluid-filled spheres and 80,000 lumens of instant light) read as lessons paid for in earlier escapes.

The description is blunter than the procedures: it prefers victims aged 10 to 25, cripples them by wrecking organs, muscles or tendons, and pulls them into its pocket dimension, where it hunts for pleasure rather than hunger, keeps many alive for long stretches, plays with them, and sometimes lets them go only to chase them again. The photo caption of an agent who lived for one hour after two hours inside makes that concrete.

The ending is the real shock. The Foundation's recall protocol is to take someone in that same age range, break a long bone like the femur or cut the Achilles tendon, put them in the restored cell and broadcast their screams across the site, repeating the injuries every twenty minutes until 106 comes for them. It is written in exactly the same flat procedural voice as the rest, which is the point.
